catalog_quote: The results of the various approaches taken in this book show that Totoli falls under the category of Phrase Languages (Féry 2016). From what is known so far, Totoli shows no evidence of tonal specifications at the level of the word; the language does not make use of word stress nor of lexical tone. sweep_summary: Totoli (toto1304) is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title, Bracks 2024 (LangSci, CC-BY, already held by the project with a text layer), was read in full: it argues from a corpus study, a Rapid Prosody Transcription experiment and a focus experiment that Totoli has no word stress and no lexical tone, only IU right-edge boundary-tone complexes whose pitch movement sits on the penultimate syllable of the IU-final word (p.1, 25, 47, 77, 148). This contradicts the older first-hand descriptions also read in this search of works with stress in the title: Himmelmann 1991 (NUSA 33 p.51: regular penultimate word stress; pp.53-54: Totoli-specific antepenultimate rule when a high-vowel penult follows a non-high vowel, e.g. báunta, táipang, dúua; final long vowels stressed) and Himmelmann 2001 (PL 511 §3.4.8 p.73: penultimate in all Tomini-Tolitoli languages, táipang ~ taípang as variation). Himmelmann 2018 (LangSci, read) already analyses Totoli with IP edge tones and no word stress, and Gari et al. 2023 (Kandai, read) only repeats Himmelmann 1991 second-hand. Extra checks: Bracks 2021 Oceanic Linguistics 60(1):103-132 is MUSE-walled with no OA copy; its abstract (Semantic Scholar) concerns IU boundary tones only and is subsumed by the 2024 book (low priority). A Crossref query found no JIPA 'Totoli' illustration as of 2026-09-17; the Kemdikbud repository for Sofyan et al. 1991 'Struktur bahasa Totoli' is still unreachable (DNS); a 2026 Journal of Connected Speech item with the book's title (10.3138/jcspeech.2025.0005, presumably a review) could not be reached by automated download.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Per Bracks 2024 (corpus of 2861 IUs plus RPT and focus production/perception experiments): Totoli has no lexical stress and no lexical tone; the only tonal events are IU-final boundary complexes (LH-L%, H-L%, L-H%) realised over the last two syllables of the intonation unit, with the phrase-tone rise/fall on the penult of the IU-final word (on the final syllable if it has a long vowel). The older impressionistic description (Himmelmann 1991 NUSA 33: 51, 53-54; Himmelmann 2001 PL-511: 73), from elicited word lists, states regular penultimate word stress for all Tomini-Tolitoli languages including Totoli, stable under suffixation, with a Totoli-specific antepenultimate sub-rule when a penult high vowel follows a non-high vowel (báunta, gáuan, táipang) but regular penult for word-final VV (kakái, kanáu).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Bracks 2024: none (no word-level prominence). Himmelmann 2001: 73 uses 'secondary stress' only for lengthening of accented CV-reduplication syllables, marked with a grave accent.
new_statements.exceptions: Bracks: long final vowel attracts both tonal targets to the final syllable. Himmelmann 1991: antepenult stress in /a,e,o + i,u/ penult sequences (Totoli 'rule', one variable item laisna); final stress when a suffix/clitic final vowel is dropped; regular penult across morpheme boundary (mo-itom). Himmelmann 2001: suffixes shift stress to keep it penultimate, clitics do not.
new_statements.domain_note: Direct conflict between generations of description by the same research group: 1991/2001 word-list elicitation gives penultimate word stress; 2018/2024 instrumental and perceptual work reanalyses the penult prominence as an IP-final edge-tone complex and denies word stress. Bracks hedges ('from what is known so far'). Citation forms = single IUs, so isolated words surface with the rise on the penult, matching the older 'penultimate stress' impression.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Totoli proper (toto1304; Bracks's corpus from the Tolitoli-Utara stronghold villages, Himmelmann's 1991/2001 data from Totoli word lists). Himmelmann 1991 sec 2.1 and Himmelmann 2001 sec 3.4.8 are family-wide Tomini-Tolitoli statements (Lauje as default exemplar) with a Totoli-specific sub-rule in 1991 sec 2.5; no dialect split is at issue.

new_statements.reading: No word stress (and no lexical tone): all pitch events are intonation-unit right-edge boundary-tone complexes whose rise/fall is timed to the penultimate syllable of the IU-final word (p.77), which is what earlier descriptions heard as 'penultimate stress'. This directly contradicts Himmelmann 1991 (NUSA 33: 51, 53-54) and Himmelmann 2001 (PL 511: 73), which state regular penultimate word stress for Totoli with an antepenultimate sub-rule before a high-vowel penult after a non-high vowel (baunta, taipang, duua). Himmelmann's own 2018 chapter already treats Totoli with IP edge tones only. If Totoli is coded, the choice is between 'no word stress / phrase-edge prosody' (Bracks 2024, experimental, most recent) and 'penultimate with vowel-sequence antepenult exception' (Himmelmann 1991/2001, impressionistic fieldwork); Bracks 2024 is the better-evidenced statement but does not test stress in isolated words.

sources.note: p.1: Totoli is a Phrase Language; 'does not make use of word stress nor of lexical tone'; tonal specifications only at IP right edge. sources.quote: p.357: "In addition to the pitch modulation occurring in a two syllable window at the right edge of an IP, which here is interpreted as a phrase accent, there tend to be further pitch rises earlier on in an IP which are not accounted for by Figure 4. Example (4) from Totoli illustrates this."
sources.note: No Totoli-specific stress sentence; Totoli elicited examples (pp.357-362) are analysed with IP/ip edge tones only (H$, L-, H%), within the general argument (pp.350, 356) that 'what has often been described as regular penultimate stress is in fact the regular occurrence of a rising-falling edge tone combination at the end of intonational phrases' and that lexical stress is not demonstrated for Austronesian languages of Indonesia outside Papua.

sources.quote: "Stress is usually not indicated, since it regularly falls on the penultimate syllable in all Tomini-Tolitoli languages. Only the exceptions to this rule are marked. Primary stress is marked by an acute accent, secondary stress (i.e. lengthening of reduplicated syllables) by a grave accent. Most exceptions to the general stress rule are well-motivated (either a phonetically long vowel is shortened (cf. §3.4.6 above) or stress moves to the first member of a sequence of unlike vowels as in táipang 'mango', which occurs as an alternate to the regular taípang)."
sources.note: sec 3.4.8 Stress, p.73 (pdf p.95): 'Stress is usually not indicated, since it regularly falls on the penultimate syllable in all Tomini-Tolitoli languages. Only the exceptions to this rule are marked. Primary stress is marked by an acute accent, secondary stress (i.e. lengthening of reduplicated syllables) by a grave accent.' Exceptions: shortened long vowels, stress on first member of unlike-vowel sequence (táipang ~ taípang). pp.91-92: suffixes shift stress (regular penult), clitics/free forms do not.

sources.quote: p.51: "Stress placement is very regular in Tomini-Tolitoli languages and thus empirically defines the domain of (word) phonology. It falls on the penultimate syllable of a (phonological) word and 'remains' penultimate when suffixes or clitics are added. Examples: 1a) báti 'head' b) batínye 'his/her head'. Exceptions to this rule are very few in number". p.53: "In Totoli, the situation is different: the 'irregular' stress placement may be captured in a 'rule': if a high vowel occurs in the penultimate syllable directly preceded by a non-high vowel, stress is placed on the antepenultimate (i.e. on the non-high vowel)." (p.54 examples: báunta 'widow', gáuan 'garden', dúua 'two', táipang 'mango', tadíso 'old man/woman', géiga 'no'; word-final VV gets regular penultimate: kakái 'grandfather', kanáu 'aren tree')

sources.quote: Abstract: "This study analyzes intonational patterns at the right edge of the intonation unit (IU) in Totoli. Based on a corpus of (semi)spontaneous discourse, I present a model of the IU. I have identified a set of three tonal patterns marking the right-edge boundary. ... segmental content was revealed not to influence the alignment but only the shape of the tonal contours. The two main exceptions responsible for alternation are the presence of long vowels and the variability in syllabification."
sources.note: Peer-reviewed journal version of the IU analysis; likely contains an explicit statement on lexical stress in Totoli predating the book.
